question: What do we call the exact step-by-step process of how a germ enters the body and causes tissue damage?
explanation: You've got this! Pathogenesis simply maps out the story of how a disease develops, from the very first contact to the resulting tissue injury. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why is it helpful for a nurse to understand how aggressive a germ is (its virulence factors)?

options.A: To calculate the exact dosage of IV fluids required daily
options.B: To measure the patient's baseline neurological function accurately
options.C: To predict how pathogens invade host tissues and cause damage
options.D: To determine the patient's exact blood type before surgery

explanation: Great thinking! Knowing a germ's tricks helps you anticipate how it will harm the body so you can plan the best nursing care. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h1)

question: Which harmful substance is released mainly when Gram-negative bacteria break apart (lysis)?
explanation: Spot on! Endotoxins live inside the outer wall of Gram-negative bacteria and get released to spark widespread inflammation when the cell bursts. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h2)

question: A patient with a bad Gram-negative infection goes into shock. What widespread substance caused this?
explanation: Well done. When Gram-negative bacteria break down, they release lipopolysaccharide endotoxins that can trigger a dangerous wave of inflammation leading to septic shock. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h2)

question: What is the main type of white blood cell packed inside a fresh, pus-filled abscess?
explanation: You nailed it! Neutrophils are our fast-responding infection fighters, rushing to a site of acute infection and forming the bulk of what we call pus. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h3)

question: Why do blood vessels become extra leaky right at the start of an acute infection?

options.A: To promote rapid regeneration of permanent myocardial cells
options.B: To lower the local tissue temperature and prevent microbial growth
options.C: To allow immune cells and fluid to reach the injured tissue
options.D: To stop all blood circulation through the affected organ

explanation: Exactly! Loosening up those blood vessel walls lets protective fluids and white blood cells rush out to fight off the invading germs. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h3)

question: Which specific cell type forms the main building blocks of a granuloma?
explanation: Spot on! Granulomas are largely made up of specialized, activated macrophages that have taken on an epithelial-like shape to handle stubborn infections. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h4)

question: What is the body's main goal when it builds a granuloma around a germ it cannot easily destroy?

options.A: To wall off and contain the infection when it cannot be eliminated
options.B: To speed up the immediate replication rate of the invading bacteria
options.C: To convert the chronic site back into an acute purulent abscess
options.D: To dissolve all surrounding healthy tissue for rapid nutrient absorption

explanation: Brilliant! If the body can't completely clear a tough germ like tuberculosis, it builds a tight wall around it to protect the rest of your organs. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h4)

question: Infections caused by pyogenic bacteria are best known for producing which substance?
explanation: You got it! The word 'pyogenic' literally means pus-producing, as these bacteria pull in masses of neutrophils to the infection site. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h5)

question: How do bacteria that live inside host cells (intracellular) usually affect tissues differently than pus-making bacteria?

options.A: They exclusively cause liquefactive necrosis without any immune cell involvement
options.B: They survive inside host cells, often triggering mononuclear responses instead of acute pus
options.C: They reproduce only in the extracellular fluid spaces without entering cells
options.D: They prevent all forms of local inflammation from occurring in the host

explanation: Spot on! Because they hide inside our cells, they dodge standard pus-forming attacks and instead trigger a more chronic, long-term immune response. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h5)

question: What do we call the large, multi-nucleated mass formed when several infected cells fuse together?
explanation: Awesome! Certain viruses trick cell membranes into merging, creating a giant shared cell known as a syncytium. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h6)

question: Why do viral infections often leave behind tiny structures inside host cells called inclusion bodies?

options.A: They form due to excessive deposition of systemic lipids in chronic shock
options.B: They are scars left behind by migrating neutrophils during acute bacterial invasion
options.C: They represent accumulations of viral particles or viral proteins inside the cell
options.D: They indicate complete structural recovery and normal cell division

explanation: You're doing great! Inclusion bodies are essentially crowded clusters of viral parts or leftover protein building up while the virus is busy multiplying. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h6)

question: Which type of white blood cell spikes in number during a parasitic worm (helminth) infection?
explanation: Spot on! Eosinophils are your body's specialized defense team for targeting larger parasites that standard white cells can't easily swallow up. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h7)

question: Why are deep fungal infections so tough for the body to completely clear out on its own?

options.A: Their rapid production of powerful endotoxins that instantly paralyze all neutrophils
options.B: Their rigid cell walls and ability to induce protective granulomas that shield the organism
options.C: Their complete lack of any surface antigens recognized by host antibodies
options.D: Their tendency to transform rapidly into free-living viral particles

explanation: Well reasoned! Fungi have tough cell walls, and the granulomas built to contain them also end up shielding the fungus, making them hard to wipe out without proper medications. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h7)

question: When is the best time to collect wound or blood cultures in relation to starting antibiotics?
explanation: You got it! Always collect your cultures before giving antibiotics so the drugs don't kill off the germs beforehand and give you a false-negative lab result. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h8)

question: A patient with a deep tissue infection has a rising C-reactive protein (CRP) level. What does this tell you?

options.A: Bone marrow production of red blood cells has stopped
options.B: The patient is experiencing normal physiological tissue repair
options.C: The infection has been completely eradicated by the immune system
options.D: Active systemic inflammation is ongoing in the body

explanation: Spot on! CRP is an alarm protein pumped out by the liver whenever there is active, widespread inflammation going on in the body. [learn more](GST114_U2_T3#GST114_U2_T3_h8)
